question.en: How did Austria change between 1844 and 1921?

intro.en: Railways crossed the Alps, a walled capital opened up, and a revolution failed. Then an empire split in two and finally dissolved. By 1921 'Austria' meant a small republic whose borders were still being settled, partly by treaty and partly by vote. Sixteen sourced events and three longer processes trace that change, reaching well beyond present-day Austria.
Rail reached Styria before the revolutions and crossed its first mountain range after them.
In Vienna, 1848 moved from concessions in March to military defeat in October.
Vienna's fortifications gave way by imperial order to a new representative boulevard.
Defeat in 1866 was followed within a year by a new settlement with Hungary, and later by nationalist programmes inside the monarchy.
From Sarajevo to the steps of the Vienna parliament in a little over four years.
A treaty fixed the terms, and votes in Carinthia and Sopron helped settle where the state ended. In the same years, Salzburg launched a festival.

summary.en: Some 20,000 workers build the mountain railway under Carl von Ghega, in the same years that revolution and its aftermath reshape the monarchy.

when.note: The source gives years only, so both ends of this bar are approximate.

summary.en: The short-lived state runs from its proclamation in November 1918 until the Treaty of Saint-Germain ends the name and the project in September 1919.
Territory gained from Hungary becomes the Austrian state of Burgenland, while villages continue to be returned or exchanged up to 1923.

when.note: The source gives 1923 as the end. The 1921 start is approximate, taken from the year of the Sopron vote.

events.noPlaceReason: A shifting border across many villages has no single location, so there's no marker for this. See the boundary shown on the map.

summary.en: The Styrian section from Mürzzuschlag to Graz enters service, extending the Southern Railway that would later continue south towards Celje and Ljubljana.
An uprising carried by the middle classes breaks out at the Lower Austrian Landhaus. Within two days Metternich resigns, a National Guard forms and press freedom is granted.

media.title: Barricade in Vienna, 26–27 May 1848
media.creator: Joseph Heicke
media.caveat: Shows the May 1848 barricades, not the March events.

summary.en: Troops ordered out of Vienna mutiny at the Gumpendorf barracks. War Minister Latour's plan collapses, and an army under Windisch-Graetz subdues the city by the end of the month.
Built from 1848 by some 20,000 workers under Carl von Ghega, the line has 14 tunnels and 16 viaducts. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

when.note: Sources checked so far confirm the year only.

summary.en: Franz Joseph signs the handwritten decree known as 'Es ist Mein Wille', ordering the demolition of Vienna's walls and moats. It appears in the Wiener Zeitung five days later.
The first stretch of the Ringstrasse is handed over to the public, seven years to the day after a smaller stretch of road opened.
Prussian forces defeat the Austrian army in Bohemia during the Austro-Prussian War, on ground that is now in the Czech Republic.

media.title: The Battle of Königgrätz
media.creator: Georg Bleibtreu
media.caveat: A painting from three years later, from the Prussian perspective. It is not a documentary image.

events.placeNote: Marked at present-day Budapest as the seat of Hungarian politics. This is an editorial placement, because the Compromise was negotiated between Vienna and Hungary rather than at a single site.

summary.en: Franz Joseph and Deák sign the Compromise, ratified by the restored Hungarian Diet. It created the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary.

when.note: The date of ratification by the Hungarian Diet.

summary.en: After years under construction, the section across the Brenner opens, linking Tyrol by rail across the main Alpine ridge.

events.placeNote: Placed at Linz because the programme is named after the city.

summary.en: German nationalists including Victor Adler call for a German-dominated Austrian state, German as the official language, and alliance with Germany. It won little support in influential political circles.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand is killed near the Latin Bridge in Sarajevo, then part of Austria-Hungary's Bosnian condominium. Gavrilo Princip is convicted and sentenced to 20 years.

media.title: Front page of La Domenica del Corriere, 12 July 1914
media.creator: Achille Beltrame
media.caveat: A newspaper illustrator's imagined reconstruction, not a photograph.

summary.en: A day after Emperor Charles relinquishes his part in state affairs, the National Assembly declares German-Austria a republic with Karl Renner as provisional chancellor.

media.title: The proclamation of the Republic outside Parliament
media.creator: Rudolf Konopa
media.caveat: An artist's painting of the crowd, not a photograph.

summary.en: Signed at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye and in force from 16 July 1920. The treaty closed off the 'German-Austria' state and set terms for the new republic's territory.

media.title: Karl Renner addressing the delegates at the Peace Conference
media.creator: Unknown

summary.en: The festival is officially inaugurated with Reinhardt's staging of Hofmannsthal's Jedermann on the steps of Salzburg Cathedral, starring Alexander Moissi.

media.title: Hugo von Hofmannsthal
media.creator: Nicola Perscheid
media.caveat: A portrait of the author from 1910, not an image of the 1920 performance.

events.placeNote: The plebiscite covered an area of southern Carinthia. The marker sits at the regional capital and does not show where votes were cast.

summary.en: Voters in a predominantly Slovene-speaking area of southern Carinthia choose Austria over the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes: 22,025 votes to 15,279.
As former Hungarian lands become Burgenland, a contested local plebiscite keeps Sopron and eight surrounding villages in Hungary, with 65% voting for Hungary.

statement.en: The railway was constructed between 1848 and 1854 by some 20,000 workers under Carl von Ghega.

evidence.passage: The History section gives the construction years, the workforce and the director.

statement.en: German-Austria was proclaimed on 12 November 1918, and the treaty is recorded as prohibiting it on 10 September 1919.

evidence.passage: The article's summary box gives both dates.

statement.en: Villages were returned or exchanged between Austria and Hungary up to 1923, and the lands gained became the state of Burgenland.

evidence.passage: The treaty article describes the later adjustments to the line.

statement.en: The Mürzzuschlag–Graz section entered service on 24 October 1844.

evidence.passage: In its account of the line's construction, the article gives this date for the Styrian section.

statement.en: The March Revolution of 13–14 March 1848 was carried by the bourgeoisie, and its outcomes included Metternich's resignation, a National Guard and press freedom.

evidence.passage: The city's history wiki lists the outbreak at the Lower Austrian Landhaus, first deaths, destruction of factories, Metternich's resignation, the National Guard and press freedom.

statement.en: Troops mutinied at the Gumpendorf barracks from 6 October 1848, and an army under Windisch-Graetz was then formed to subdue Vienna.

evidence.passage: The entry dates the event 6–31 October 1848 and describes the mutiny, then the army formed from garrison troops, Jellačić's force and a Bohemian contingent.

statement.en: The line was built between 1848 and 1854 by some 20,000 workers under Carl von Ghega, with 14 tunnels and 16 viaducts.

evidence.passage: The History section gives the construction years, the workforce, the designer and the count of engineering works.

statement.en: The railway opened in 1854 and has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1998.

evidence.passage: The German article's lead gives the opening year and the inscription.
The English article gives the same inscription year. Both are language editions of one reference work, so this is weak corroboration.

statement.en: The imperial handwritten decree was signed on 20 December 1857 and published in the Wiener Zeitung on 25 December.

evidence.passage: The entry calls the decree the official starting signal and notes it was drafted in the Ministry of the Interior.

statement.en: The decree, known as 'Es ist Mein Wille', ordered the demolition of the city walls and moats.

evidence.passage: The article names the decree and its demolition order.

statement.en: The first section of the Ringstrasse opened to the public on 1 May 1865.

evidence.passage: The entry also records a small stretch of road, from the former Rotenturmtor to the Ferdinandsbrücke, opened on 1 May 1858. 'First opening' therefore depends on what counts as the Ringstrasse.

statement.en: The battle was fought on 3 July 1866 as part of the Austro-Prussian War and ended in a Prussian victory.

evidence.passage: The article's summary box gives the date, the wider war, the location and the result.

statement.en: Franz Joseph and Ferenc Deák signed the Compromise, and the restored Diet of Hungary ratified it on 29 May 1867.

evidence.passage: The article gives the signatories and the ratification date.

statement.en: The Compromise was arranged and legitimated by a narrow part of Hungarian society, with under 8% of the population holding the vote.

evidence.passage: The franchise figure is a statistic. The framing that the settlement lacked wider legitimacy is an interpretation, and the original scholarship has not yet been linked here.

statement.en: The section under construction was finally opened on 24 August 1867.

evidence.passage: The article gives the opening date in its history of the line.

statement.en: The framers of the 1882 programme sought a German-dominated Austrian state, out of fear that Slavs were overrunning the German element of the monarchy.

evidence.passage: The article describes the programme's goal and the fears behind it. These were the framers' views, and the app does not present them as fact about the monarchy.

statement.en: The programme never gained much support in influential political circles.

evidence.passage: An assessment of its reception, reported here without its underlying scholarship.

statement.en: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated on 28 June 1914 near the Latin Bridge, Sarajevo.

evidence.passage: The summary box gives the date and location, in the Condominium of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Austria-Hungary.

statement.en: Gavrilo Princip was found guilty of murder and high treason, and was sentenced to 20 years because he was too young to be executed.

evidence.passage: The article reports the verdict and sentence.

statement.en: On 12 November 1918 the National Assembly declared German-Austria a republic and named Karl Renner provisional chancellor.

evidence.passage: The article gives the date of the declaration and Renner's appointment.

statement.en: On 11 November 1918 Charles recognised the Austrian people's right to determine the form of the state, and left Schönbrunn for Eckartsau that day.

evidence.passage: The article describes the carefully worded proclamation and the family's move from Schönbrunn.

statement.en: The treaty was signed on 10 September 1919 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye and took effect on 16 July 1920.

evidence.passage: The article's summary box gives the signing date, place and effective date.

statement.en: The treaty is recorded as prohibiting the state of German-Austria.

evidence.passage: The article's summary box gives this as the state's end, dated 10 September 1919.

statement.en: Territories gained from Hungary were organised as the Austrian state of Burgenland, and some villages were returned or exchanged up to 1923.

evidence.passage: The treaty article describes the outcome and later adjustments to the line.

statement.en: The festival was officially inaugurated on 22 August 1920 with Jedermann on the steps of Salzburg Cathedral.

evidence.passage: The article names Reinhardt as director, Hofmannsthal as author and Moissi as lead.

statement.en: On 10 October 1920, 22,025 votes (59.1%) went to Austria and 15,279 (40.9%) to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

evidence.passage: The Results section gives the totals for the plebiscite area.

statement.en: A local plebiscite on 14 December 1921 decided Sopron's status, with 65% voting for Hungary. The source itself calls the vote controversial.

evidence.passage: The article reports the vote and the Venice Protocol mediation behind it. The competing accounts of the vote's fairness are not yet linked here.
